notes.meaning: While Israel camped at Shittim, the men began committing sexual sins with the women of Moab. This failure happened right on the border of the promised land after God had shielded them from Balaam's curses. Instead of trusting God, the people gave in to temptation and brought trouble on themselves.

The Moabite women invited the Israelite men to attend feasts for their false gods. Eating the meat from these sacrifices was a way of sharing in the worship of those idols. By joining in the meals, the men turned their backs on the true God.

The people joined themselves to Baal of Peor, a local idol whose worship involved shameful and corrupt rituals. By yoking themselves to this false god, they broke their sacred bond with the Lord. This blatant disloyalty made the Lord extremely angry.

The Lord told Moses to arrest the ringleaders of this rebellion and have them publicly executed in broad daylight. Exposing the guilty leaders to open shame satisfied God's justice. Carrying out this judgment was necessary to turn God's fierce anger away from the rest of the nation.

Moses commanded the judges of Israel to put to death every man under their care who had joined in worshiping Baal of Peor. Each leader was responsible for enforcing God's law among the people he governed. They had to act decisively to remove the evil from the camp.

An Israelite man boldly marched a Midianite woman into the camp right in front of Moses and the community. The faithful people were already weeping in grief and repentance at the entrance to the sacred tent because of the outbreak of God's anger. This man's open sin showed complete contempt for God and his grieving neighbors.

When Phinehas the priest saw this defiant act, he grabbed a spear, followed the couple into the inner room of the tent, and killed both of them. His swift action brought a sudden halt to the deadly plague that was ravaging the people. God honored this deed because it put an end to the public defiance in Israel.

differ.view: Calvin argued that Phinehas acted by an extraordinary inward command from the Holy Spirit, meaning private persons cannot take the law into their own hands without such direct divine authorization.
Wesley emphasized that Phinehas held official authority as a ruler, acted with Moses' consent in line with the command to slay offenders, and was guided by the Holy Spirit.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: Modern teachers emphasize that under the covenant where idolatry and adultery carried the death penalty, Phinehas acted as a principled protector whose decisive intervention saved thousands of lives.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic commentators note that Phinehas was either a legitimate judge or acting by direct divine inspiration, warning that his deed gives no license for private vigilante violence.

notes.meaning: Even though the judgment was halted, twenty-four thousand people died during this disaster. This heavy toll showed the terrible cost of turning away from God. It stood as a permanent warning about the danger of spiritual unfaithfulness.

The Lord spoke to Moses and praised Phinehas for turning His anger away from the Israelites. Phinehas shared God's own deep passion for holiness and refused to tolerate evil among the people. Because he took action, God did not wipe out the entire nation in His jealousy.

God directed Moses to announce that He was giving Phinehas a special covenant of peace. This was a promise of divine favor, safety, and friendship from the Lord. Phinehas had restored peace between God and Israel, and his family would now serve as guardians of that peace.

God pledged that the priesthood would stay permanently in the family line of Phinehas and his descendants. This honor rewarded his devotion to God and his act of making atonement—removing guilt and turning aside God's wrath—for the nation. His faithful stand secured a lasting spiritual legacy.

differ.view: Wesley taught that this promise was conditional on continued obedience, which explained why the high priesthood was later temporarily transferred to Eli's family.
Keil and Delitzsch maintained that God granted the priesthood in an irrevocable form because the Lord never breaks His covenants.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Modern critical scholars view this promise as a later text created to defend the exclusive claim of Zadok's descendants to the high priesthood.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic commentary explains that God granted a perpetual right to the office, but that individual descendants could still forfeit the privilege through wicked behavior.

notes.meaning: The slain Israelite man was Zimri, a prince from the tribe of Simeon, and the woman was Cozbi, the daughter of a Midianite leader. Recording their names and noble positions showed that God's justice does not spare anyone because of wealth or rank. Their high status only made their open defiance more shameful and unforgettable.

The Lord commanded Moses to treat the Midianites as enemies and attack them. They had deliberately plotted Israel's ruin by tricking them into sexual immorality and the worship of Baal of Peor through women like Cozbi. God required this holy war to punish the deceivers who had drawn His people into deadly sin.
